title: Neutral Tones: date and publication
short: Dated 1867, when Hardy was in his mid-twenties; first published thirty years later in Wessex Poems (1898).
body: Hardy dated the poem 1867, when he was a young architect's assistant writing poetry that magazines rejected. It remained unpublished until his first collection, Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1898), which he illustrated with his own drawings (hence the bracketed note of a sketch in this text). It is widely considered the finest of his early poems. The woman addressed is not identified, and attempts to link the poem to a particular early love remain speculation. Its date makes it a remarkable anticipation of the bleak, plain style of Hardy's later verse.

title: Title and colour: 'Neutral Tones'
short: The title borrows a painter's term for greys and muted colours; the poem is drained of colour, from white sun to gray leaves.
body: 'Neutral tint' and 'neutral tones' were watercolourists' terms for greys and dull mixtures without strong hue, and Hardy, trained as an architect and a capable draughtsman, knew this vocabulary. The poem's palette is accordingly white (the sun), gray (the leaves), and the implied browns of the 'starving sod'. 'Neutral' also suggests emotional deadness: neither love nor open hatred, but exhausted indifference. The title therefore announces both the scene's visual monotony and the emotional state of the couple.

title: the sun was white
short: A pale winter sun without warmth or colour, as if drained of life.
body: In winter the sun can appear as a pale white disc, giving light without warmth. Hardy's choice of 'white' rather than gold or red removes the sun's usual associations with life and joy. The line also inverts the conventional pathetic fallacy: rather than nature sympathising with lovers, it seems to share in the punishment of the scene. The flat, mostly monosyllabic diction of the opening line sets the plain, unemphatic tone of the whole poem.

title: as though chidden of God
short: 'Chidden' is an old past participle of 'chide', to rebuke; 'of God' means 'by God'. The sun looks pale as if scolded.
body: 'Chide' means to scold or reprove, and 'chidden' is its archaic past participle; 'of' in the sense 'by' is also old-fashioned. The sun has been rebuked by God, a simile that hints at a universe under divine disfavour rather than benevolence. It is the first of two references to God in the poem: by the last stanza the sun has become 'God-curst', an escalation from reprimand to curse that measures how the speaker's bitterness has hardened over time.

title: the starving sod
short: The winter turf, hungry and lifeless; 'sod' is grass-covered earth.
body: 'Sod' is the surface of the ground with grass growing on it. 'Starving' personifies the earth as underfed and suffering, matching the deprivation of the relationship. The alliteration of s across 'sun', 'starving' and 'sod' links sky and ground in a single bleak picture. The few leaves lying on it suggest that the year, like the love, has spent itself.

title: They had fallen from an ash
short: The leaves come from an ash tree; the tree's name may also suggest the ashes of burnt-out passion.
body: The ash is a common English tree, among the last to come into leaf and the first to drop its leaves. Hardy's specificity is typical of his observant naturalism. Some readers hear a secondary suggestion in the word: ashes are what remains after a fire, and the love here has burnt itself out. Whether intended or not, the grey colour of the leaves supports the association, and the tree returns in the final stanza as part of the remembered scene.

title: Over tedious riddles solved years ago
short: Her eyes move over him with boredom, as over puzzles long solved; editions differ; many print 'riddles of years ago'.
body: The simile says that she looks at him without interest, as one glances over old puzzles whose answers are already known: he is no longer a mystery to her. 'Tedious' sharpens the insult. The line exists in two versions: this text, following the 1898 Wessex Poems, reads 'riddles solved years ago', while many modern printings give 'riddles of years ago'; check a critical edition for which reading is Hardy's later one. The variant changes the sense slightly, from riddles already solved (nothing left to discover) to riddles from long ago (stale). Editors such as Gibson record Hardy's revisions in the textual apparatus.

title: On which lost the more by our love
short: The words they exchanged were about which of them had lost more by loving: a quarrel over who has been more harmed.
body: The compressed syntax means: some words passed between us about which of us had lost more because of our love. The love is spoken of as a loss rather than a gain, and the conversation is a weary contest of grievances, 'played' back and forth like a game. Some readers take 'played' to suggest triviality or even a cruel game. The line ends the second stanza on an irregular, stumbling rhythm.

title: The smile on your mouth was the deadest thing / Alive enough
short: A paradox: her smile was the most lifeless thing that still had just enough life in it to die.
body: The oxymoron is the poem's most memorable conceit. The smile is dead yet 'Alive enough to have strength to die': it is so near death that its only remaining vitality is the power to expire. The effect is of a gesture of affection emptied of meaning, persisting only as a mechanical movement. Commentators have often singled out this line for the way it compresses the poem's theme, the death of love while the lovers still live, into a single image.

title: Like an ominous bird a-wing
short: Her bitter grin passes over her face like a bird of ill omen in flight; 'a-wing' is an old form meaning 'on the wing'.
body: Birds were traditionally read as omens (as in Roman augury), and a bird of ill omen, such as a raven or crow, foretells misfortune. The grin of bitterness flits across the smile as such a bird crosses the sky, an ominous sign of what is to come. 'A-wing' uses the archaic prefix a- (from Old English on) as in 'afoot' or 'asleep'. The stanza ends with an ellipsis in the original, as if the omen remains unspoken.

title: Since then, keen lessons that love deceives
short: The last stanza moves forward in time: later experiences of love's deception have fixed that scene in his memory as an emblem.
body: The first three stanzas describe a single winter day; the fourth reflects from later years ('Since then'). Subsequent 'keen' (sharp, painful) lessons that love deceives and 'wrings with wrong' have caused the remembered scene to come back to him whenever love fails. The syntax is that these lessons 'have shaped to me' her face, the sun, the tree and the pond: the image has become a permanent emblem of disillusion. The poem is circular, returning to the pond and leaves of the opening. The alliteration of 'wrings with wrong' mimics a twisting pain.

title: the God-curst sun
short: The 'chidden' sun of stanza one has become 'God-curst': memory has hardened rebuke into curse.
body: Hardy repeats the elements of the first stanza in a list (face, sun, tree, pond), but the sun now carries a compound epithet that intensifies the earlier simile. Being 'curst' by God is far stronger than being 'chidden'. The change suggests how bitterness has grown over the years, and the hyphenated compound is a characteristic feature of Hardy's diction. The phrase also points toward Hardy's lifelong scepticism about divine benevolence, though here it remains part of a personal, not a philosophical, statement.

title: And a pond edged with grayish leaves
short: The last line returns to the opening scene, closing the circle; quatrains rhymed abba with a shorter, indented last line.
body: Each stanza has four lines rhymed abba, with a mainly four-beat line that mixes iambs and anapaests, and an indented fourth line. The envelope rhyme encloses each stanza, and the poem as a whole is enclosed by the return to the pond and leaves. The slight change from 'gray' to 'grayish' adds vagueness, as of a memory blurred by time. Critics often note the poem's circular structure as an image of the lover's inability to escape the moment of disillusion.
